claim: Candida albicans causes severe invasive candidiasis.
source: Candida albicans causes severe invasive candidiasis.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about C. albicans infections.

claim: C. albicans infection requires the virulence factor candidalysin (CL) which damages target cell membranes.
source: C. albicans infection requires the virulence factor candidalysin (CL) which damages target cell membranes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CL readily assembled into polymers in solution.
source: Unexpectedly, CL readily assembled into polymers in solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental techniques including SDS-PAGE, IM-MS, analytical ultracentrifugation, mass photometry, TEM, and AFM data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The basic structural unit in polymer formation is a CL oligomer.
source: We propose that the basic structural unit in polymer formation is a CL oligomer, which is sequentially added into a string configuration that can close into a loop.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data including IM-MS, AFM, and modeling results.

claim: CL oligomers are sequentially added into a string configuration that can close into a loop.
source: We propose that the basic structural unit in polymer formation is a CL oligomer, which is sequentially added into a string configuration that can close into a loop.
evidence: This is supported by AFM imaging showing linear polymers and loops, and by volume analysis showing stepwise growth.

claim: CL loops spontaneously insert into the membrane to become pores.
source: CL loops appear to spontaneously insert into the membrane to become pores.
evidence: This is supported by AFM data showing loops in solution and pores in membranes with similar dimensions, and by detergent removal experiments.

claim: The G4W CL mutation inhibited the formation of polymers in solution.
source: A CL mutation (G4W) inhibited the formation of polymers in solution and prevented pore formation in synthetic lipid systems.
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry and AFM data showing reduced polymer formation for G4W variant.

claim: The G4W CL mutation prevented pore formation in synthetic lipid systems.
source: A CL mutation (G4W) inhibited the formation of polymers in solution and prevented pore formation in synthetic lipid systems.
evidence: This is supported by AFM imaging of membranes and liposome dye release assays showing no pore formation or membrane disruption by G4W.

claim: G4W CL failed to activate the danger response pathway in epithelial cells.
source: Epithelial cell studies showed that G4W CL failed to activate the danger response pathway, a hallmark of the pathogenic effect of CL.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing no increase in c-Fos expression or MKP1 phosphorylation in cells treated with G4W.

claim: CL polymerization in solution is a necessary step for the damage of cellular membranes.
source: These results indicate that CL polymerization in solution is a necessary step for the damage of cellular membranes.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the G4W mutation data showing that preventing polymerization prevents membrane damage and cellular responses.

claim: CL pores exist as simple depressions and more complex pores.
source: Analysis of CL pores by atomic force microscopy revealed co-existence of simple depressions and more complex pores, which are likely formed by CL assembled in an alternate oligomer orientation.
evidence: This is supported by AFM imaging showing two types of pores: unrimmed and rimmed pores with different characteristics.

claim: Complex pores are likely formed by CL assembled in an alternate oligomer orientation.
source: Analysis of CL pores by atomic force microscopy revealed co-existence of simple depressions and more complex pores, which are likely formed by CL assembled in an alternate oligomer orientation.
evidence: This is inferred from modeling and AFM data comparing unrimmed and rimmed pores, suggesting a 90-degree rotation of the 8-mer subunits.

claim: The structural rearrangement represents a maturation mechanism that stabilizes pore formation.
source: We propose that this structural rearrangement represents a maturation mechanism that stabilizes pore formation to achieve more robust cellular damage.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM time-series data showing that rimmed pores are more stable than unrimmed pores.

claim: CL uses a previously unknown mechanism to damage membranes, whereby pre-assembly of CL loops in solution leads to formation of membrane pores.
source: To summarize, CL uses a previously unknown mechanism to damage membranes, whereby pre-assembly of CL loops in solution leads to formation of membrane pores.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence showing polymerization in solution and subsequent membrane insertion.

claim: Fungal infections are responsible for high morbidity burden around the world.
source: Fungal infections are responsible for high morbidity burden around the world (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2012.

claim: Candida albicans is one of the most serious fungal threats to human health.
source: Candida albicans is one of the most serious fungal threats to human health.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and the context provided in the introduction.

claim: C. albicans is part of the commensal flora.
source: This pathogen is part of the commensal flora, but can infect the skin, mouth, vagina, and gut, both in healthy and immunocompromised individuals.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about C. albicans.

claim: C. albicans can infect the skin, mouth, vagina, and gut in both healthy and immunocompromised individuals.
source: This pathogen is part of the commensal flora, but can infect the skin, mouth, vagina, and gut, both in healthy and immunocompromised individuals.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about C. albicans infections.

claim: C. albicans causes invasive candidiasis, an infection of the blood, heart, and other organs.
source: Additionally, C. albicans causes invasive candidiasis, an infection of the blood, heart, and other organs, which is common in hospitalized patients (Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015.

claim: Invasive candidiasis is common in hospitalized patients.
source: Additionally, C. albicans causes invasive candidiasis, an infection of the blood, heart, and other organs, which is common in hospitalized patients (Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015.

claim: Invasive candidiasis causes high rates of mortality (~50%), even when patients are treated with antifungal therapy.
source: Invasive candidiasis causes high rates of mortality (~50%), even when patients are treated with antifungal therapy (Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015.

claim: C. albicans causes toxicity by secreting a peptide toxin named candidalysin (CL) onto the surface of epithelial cells.
source: It has been recently discovered that C. albicans causes toxicity by secreting onto the surface of epithelial cells a peptide toxin named candidalysin (CL) (Moyes et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moyes et al., 2016.

claim: CL binds to the plasma membrane of target human epithelial cells.
source: This virulence factor binds to the plasma membrane of target human epithelial cells and compromises the permeability barrier, causing uncontrolled Ca2+ influx and release of cellular proteins on to the extracellular medium (Naglik et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Naglik et al., 2019.

claim: CL compromises the permeability barrier of epithelial cells, causing uncontrolled Ca2+ influx and release of cellular proteins.
source: This virulence factor binds to the plasma membrane of target human epithelial cells and compromises the permeability barrier, causing uncontrolled Ca2+ influx and release of cellular proteins on to the extracellular medium (Naglik et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Naglik et al., 2019.

claim: Cellular damage caused by CL activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators.
source: The resulting cellular damage activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators (Naglik et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2018b), which participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Naglik et al., 2019 and Richardson et al., 2018b.

claim: Pro-inflammatory mediators released in response to CL participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
source: The resulting cellular damage activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators (Naglik et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2018b), which participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and established immunological knowledge.

claim: CL attacks the membrane of mononuclear phagocytes.
source: Furthermore, CL plays a second pathogenic role, as it also attacks the membrane of mononuclear phagocytes which would otherwise fight the fungal infection (Kasper et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kasper et al., 2018.

claim: CL is necessary for infection by C. albicans.
source: CL is necessary for infection by C. albicans (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CL activity is a promising avenue to fight infection of C. albicans.
source: Therefore, pharmacological inhibition of CL activity is a promising avenue to fight infection of this human pathogen.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the necessity of CL for infection.

claim: The development of drugs to counter the action of CL is hampered by the lack of understanding of how this peptide damages membranes.
source: However, the development of drugs to counter the action of CL is hampered by the lack of understanding of how this peptide damages membranes.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the relationship between mechanistic understanding and drug development.

claim: CL self-assembles in solution.
source: This result suggests that CL self-assembles in solution, and we hypothesized that this event might be related to its ability to damage cellular membranes.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data showing oligomeric bands in Figure 1A.

claim: IM-MS analysis of CL revealed several oligomeric species.
source: IM-MS analysis of CL revealed several oligomeric species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the IM-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mass spectral peak at m/z 3311 corresponds to a nominal oligomer-to-charge ratio (n/z) of 1/1.
source: The mass spectral peak at m/z 3311, which corresponds to a nominal oligomer-to-charge ratio (n/z) of 1/1, was notable due to its high intensity when compared to the surrounding oligomers.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the IM-MS data in Figure 1B.

claim: The longest arrival time feature in the ATD corresponds to an 8-mer with z = +8.
source: We conservatively assigned the longest arrival time feature (salmon) as an 8-mer with z = +8.
evidence: This assignment is based on analysis of isotopic spacing and drift time data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fastest arrival time species is proposed to be a large oligomer resulting from the self-assembly of the 8-mer.
source: Since a species with a high charge will travel faster than one with a lower charge, the fastest arrival time species (green) is proposed to be a large oligomer resulting from the self-assembly of the 8-mer.
evidence: This is inferred from the IM-MS data and principles of ion mobility.

claim: CL adopts helical structure in solution.
source: Given that CL adopts helical structure in solution (Moyes et al., 2016), we built an atomistic model of the 8-mer by aligning CL's sequence into the eight-helix coiled coil formed by CC-Type2-II (PDB ID 6G67).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moyes et al., 2016.

claim: The theoretical collisional cross-section of the CL 8-mer model (2500 Å2) agrees with the experimental value of 2567 Å2.
source: After the resulting structure was energy minimized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the theoretical collisional cross-section of the model, 2500 Å2, agreed with the experimental value of 2567 Å2.
evidence: This comparison between theoretical and experimental values supports the validity of the 8-mer model.

claim: Analytical ultracentrifugation data identifies populations of increasingly larger CL oligomers.
source: Analytical ultracentrifugation data identifies populations of increasingly larger CL oligomers.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mass photometry data of CL shows oligomeric species with masses corresponding to 2, 3, 4, 8, 13, and 22 CL 8-mers.
source: Data distribution was best fit with six Gaussian populations (shown as blue lines, and summary fit is the black line). The mass of the peaks agree with the expected mass for 2, 3, 4, 8, 13, and 22 CL 8-mers (similar to a Fibonacci sequence).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the mass photometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CL does not form amorphous aggregates, but instead assembles into linear structures.
source: We first performed negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and observed that CL does not form amorphous aggregates, but instead assembles into linear structures (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the TEM data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TEM data revealed a basic structural unit that grows in a step-wise fashion into polymers.
source: The TEM data revealed a basic structural unit, which seemed to grow in a step-wise fashion into polymers (Figure 2A, side panels).
evidence: This is observed in the TEM images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Longer CL polymers curve and in some cases close in on themselves, forming a loop with diameter ≥10 nm.
source: The longer polymers curved, and in some cases closed in on themselves, forming a loop with diameter ≥10 nm.
evidence: This is observed in the TEM data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AFM images of CL adsorbed onto mica in buffer confirmed that CL polymerizes and can form loops.
source: AFM images of CL adsorbed onto mica in buffer (Figure 2B) agreed with the TEM results and confirmed that CL polymerizes and can form loops.
evidence: This is directly observed in the AFM data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The bending stiffness of CL polymers, calculated from persistence length analysis, is Lp = 9 nm±2 nm.
source: The bending stiffness of CL polymers was calculated from AFM images through persistence length, Lp, analysis (Lp = 9 nm±2 nm, N=100, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from AFM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bending stiffness of linear CL polymers is significantly lower than other biological polymers, like actin fibers.
source: The bending stiffness of linear CL polymers is significantly lower than other biological polymers, like actin fibers (Gittes et al., 1993), explaining the ability of CL polymers to close into loops.
evidence: This comparison is made with cited literature on actin fibers.

claim: The volume histogram of CL features from AFM has a sharp peak and a long tail.
source: Examination of AFM images containing thousands of particles yielded a volume distribution with a sharp peak and a long tail (Figure 2C), which resembles the distribution observed in the MP data (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the AFM volume histogram in Figure 2C.

claim: The AFM volume histogram resembles the distribution observed in the MP data.
source: Examination of AFM images containing thousands of particles yielded a volume distribution with a sharp peak and a long tail (Figure 2C), which resembles the distribution observed in the MP data (Figure 1E).
evidence: This comparison between AFM and MP data supports the robustness of the observations.

claim: The AFM volume histogram was deconvolved by fitting Gaussian distributions, revealing a primary peak and several larger sub-populations.
source: The AFM volume histogram was deconvolved by fitting Gaussian distributions, revealing a primary peak and several larger sub-populations of larger volumes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis of Figure 2C.

claim: The volume increased in approximately constant steps between the populations.
source: The volume increased in approximately constant steps between the populations (see side panels of Figure 2B), confirming that a basic intermediate oligomer grew first by dimerization, followed by sequential addition to further increase linear polymer length.
evidence: This is observed in the AFM data and volume analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The height histogram of individual CL particles from AFM yielded two peaks, with heights of 3.2±0.4 nm and 4.6±0.5 nm.
source: We measured the height of the individual particles observed by AFM, and the resulting histogram (Figure 2D) yielded two peaks, with heights of 3.2±0.4 nm and 4.6±0.5 nm.
evidence: This is directly measured from AFM data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The bimodal height distribution indicates two orientations (vertical and horizontal) of the basic structural unit.
source: We reasoned that the bimodal height distribution could indicate two orientations (vertical and horizontal) of the basic structural unit that serves as an intermediate oligomer (Figure 2B inset, labeled '1'), which is probably the CL 8-mer identified by IM-MS (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the AFM height data and comparison with the 8-mer model.

claim: Simulated AFM images of the CL 8-mer in horizontal or vertical orientations yielded heights of 3.3 nm and 4.8 nm.
source: We tested this possibility by using the CL 8-mer model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to generate simulated AFM images through morphological dilation of the estimated tip geometry for the 8-mer, either on its horizontal or vertical orientations (Figure 2D, insets). We found good agreement between the simulation [heights of 3.3 nm and 4.8 nm] and the two experimental peaks shown in Figure 2D.
evidence: This is based on AFM simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: The volume of the modeled 8-mer in the horizontal orientation agrees with the value of the basic AFM structural unit.
source: Interestingly, the volume of the modeled 8-mer in the horizontal orientation additionally agrees within uncertainty with the value of the basic AFM structural unit (Figure 2C inset).
evidence: This comparison between model and experimental data supports the 8-mer hypothesis.

claim: CL assembles into an 8-mer in solution that acts as an intermediate step in the self-assembly process.
source: Taken together, these results support the notion that CL assembles into an 8-mer in solution that acts as an intermediate step in the self-assembly process.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence including IM-MS, AFM, and modeling.

claim: Polymer growth of CL 8-mers in the horizontal orientation can occur by side-by-side or head-to-toe addition.
source: Polymer growth of CL 8-mers in the horizontal orientation (lying flat on a surface) can occur by addition of a second 8-mer in two fundamental modes, side-by-side or head-to-toe.
evidence: This is a logical inference about possible assembly modes.

claim: Modeling of head-to-toe assembly of two, three, and four 8-mers shows agreement between simulated and experimental AFM volumes.
source: When we modeled the latter arrangement for the assembly of two, three, and four head-to-toe 8-mers (Figure 2C, inset), we found agreement between the simulated and experimental AFM volumes (Figure 2C, inset; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This comparison between simulations and experimental data supports the head-to-toe assembly model.

claim: A CL polymer is formed when a basic subunit is aligned in the longest dimension and grows by sequential head-to-toe addition of additional subunits.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that a CL polymer is formed when a basic subunit, which our results suggest is an 8-mer, is aligned in the longest dimension, and grows by sequential head-to-toe addition of additional subunits.
evidence: This conclusion is based on AFM volume analysis and modeling.

claim: CL forms membrane pores.
source: It has been proposed that CL forms membrane pores (Moyes et al., 2016), but such structures have never been observed.
evidence: This is supported by AFM imaging showing pore-like depressions in lipid bilayers in the presence of CL.

claim: In the presence of CL, DOPC bilayers exhibited punctate depressions commonly associated with pores.
source: We performed AFM imaging on supported lipid bilayers made of DOPC (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) to gain insights into how CL causes membrane disruption. We observed that in the presence of CL, bilayers indeed exhibited punctate depressions commonly associated with pores (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in AFM images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (unrimmed) and complex pores surrounded by a rim (rimmed).
source: The CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (Figure 3A), and complex pores surrounded by a rim of discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in AFM images shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Rimmed pores are surrounded by discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface.
source: The CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (Figure 3A), and complex pores surrounded by a rim of discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is measured from AFM data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer.
source: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
source: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of pore diffusion.

claim: Rimmed pores generally have a smaller area than unrimmed pores.
source: Rimmed pores generally have a smaller area than unrimmed pores (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claim: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2.
source: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2 (Figure 3C, gray), while the rimmed pores have a narrower distribution, and an area peak at 26 nm2 (Figure 3C, black).
evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claim: Rimmed pores have a narrower area distribution, with an area peak at 26 nm2.
source: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2 (Figure 3C, gray), while the rimmed pores have a narrower distribution, and an area peak at 26 nm2 (Figure 3C, black).
evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claim: Unrimmed pores show dynamic behavior, with large variations over time.
source: A representative unrimmed pore (Figure 3D, top row) shows dynamic behavior, with large variations over time. The pore depth visibly varies, flickering between deep and shallow states.
evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Rimmed pores appear deeper and are more stable than unrimmed pores.
source: On the other hand, the rimmed pore (Figure 3D, bottom row) appears deeper, and is more stable, as shown by the constant profile over time (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The presence of the rim endows the pore with increased stability.
source: While the two types of pores are likely to cause membrane permeabilization, we propose that the presence of the rim endows the pore with increased stability, which could potentially be a mechanism to afford CL pores with enhanced membrane damaging capabilities.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rimmed pores are more stable over time.

claim: There are strong similarities between the shape and size of the loops that CL forms in the absence of membrane and the unrimmed membrane pores.
source: We noticed that there were strong similarities between the shape and size of the loops that CL forms in the absence of membrane and the unrimmed membrane pores (Figure 3C, compare blue and gray lines).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the area distributions in Figure 3C.

claim: CL loops can insert into membranes and become unrimmed pores.
source: This agreement led us to hypothesize that CL loops could insert into membranes and become unrimmed pores.
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by observations of loops and pores after lipid dissociation, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Loops were observed where pores were previously present after lipid dissociation.
source: Upon imaging the exact same area again, we observed features similar to the CL polymers and loops detected in the absence of lipid bilayers. Indeed, loops, often inter-connected, were observed where pores were previously present (see blue arrows).
evidence: This is directly observed in AFM images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption.
source: Linear features similar to the CL polymers observed for solution samples were also present, which had been previously obscured by the presence of a bilayer. This observation indicates that linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption, but when they close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When linear polymers close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
source: This observation indicates that linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption, but when they close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Detergent (DβM) was used to forcibly remove lipid bilayers.
source: In order to replicate these spontaneous events in a deterministic manner, we used the mild detergent dodecyl beta-D-maltoside (DβM) to remove the lipid bilayer (Milhiet et al., 2006; Rinia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by citations.

claim: DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support.
source: Control experiments showed that DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support, but did not dissociate the CL polymers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1);
evidence: This is shown in control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DβM did not dissociate the CL polymers.
source: Control experiments showed that DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support, but did not dissociate the CL polymers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1);
evidence: This is shown in control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Detergent treatment might reduce the fraction of polymers that close into a loop.
source: however, our data suggest that detergent treatment might reduce the fraction of polymers that close into a loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is suggested by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vertical 8-mer orientation is favored in the presence of lipid membranes.
source: However, the increase in taller features could also be an indication that the vertical 8-mer orientation (Figure 2D) is favored in the presence of lipid membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the height histogram comparison in Figure 4C.

claim: Loops found in solution assemble in a head-to-toe fashion.
source: Comparison between the experimental inner areas and the models (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggest that the loops found in solution, similar to the linear polymers, assemble into a head-to-toe fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison between experimental data and models shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The average loop is composed of six head-to-toe 8-mers, for a mass of 159 kDa.
source: The average loop would be composed of six head-to-toe 8-mers, for a mass (159 kDa) that corresponds with the start of the tail in the MP distribution (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from modeling and comparison with mass photometry data.

claim: CL forms an α-helical structure in solution.
source: Figure 5B shows that CL forms, as expected (Moyes et al., 2016), an α-helical structure in solution, as evidenced by the spectral minima at 208 and 222 nm.
evidence: This is shown by circular dichroism data in Figure 5B and supported by citation.

claim: The presence of lipid vesicles promotes modest additional helix formation in CL.
source: We also observed that the presence of lipid vesicles promotes modest additional helix formation, possibly by growth of the α-helix and its ends.
evidence: This is observed in the CD data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The OCD data of CL indicate that the predominant orientation of helices in membranes is transmembrane.
source: The OCD data of CL displayed low intensity, and a minimum at ~225 nm and a maximum at ~195 nm, similarly to the expected result for TM helices (Alves et al., 2018; Stefanski et al., 2021). The OCD spectrum therefore indicates that the predominant orientation of helices in CL in membranes was inserted across the membrane, in a TM orientation.
evidence: This is shown by OCD data in Figure 5C and comparison with expected spectra for TM helices.

claim: The OCD spectrum supports the presence of a population of α-helices oriented along the plane of the membrane.
source: However, the presence of a depression at ~210 nm agrees with the presence of a population of α-helices oriented along the plane of the membrane, like those expected for the unrimmed pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the OCD spectrum shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The OCD result supports the presence of a combination of rimmed and unrimmed CL pores with the respective helical orientations predicted by the AFM modeling.
source: Therefore, the OCD result supports the presence of a combination of rimmed and unrimmed CL pores with the respective helical orientations predicted by the AFM modeling.
evidence: This conclusion integrates OCD data with AFM modeling results.

claim: A head-to-toe assembly of a parallel helical bundle implies interaction between the N-terminal helical ends of an 8-mer with the C-termini of the adjacent subunit.
source: A head-to-toe assembly of a parallel helical bundle implies interaction between the N-terminal (Nt) helical ends of an 8-mer with the C-termini of the adjacent subunit (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the head-to-toe assembly model.

claim: The 8-mer model predicts that the N-terminus is slightly kinked at residue G4.
source: Our 8-mer model predicts that the Nt is slightly kinked at residue G4 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the model structure in Figure 6A.

claim: Glycine residues confer flexibility to α-helices.
source: Since glycine residues confer flexibility to α-helices (Choy et al., 2003), we reasoned that the mutation of residue G4 (Figure 6A) might affect CL self-assembly.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Choy et al., 2003.

claim: G4W formed few large assemblies in solution.
source: We first tested the ability of the resulting G4W CL variant to polymerize in solution using MP, and observed that G4W formed few large assemblies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in the mass photometry data in Figure 6B.

claim: The I9A variant self-assembles efficiently in solution.
source: The MP results show that the I9A variant, on the other hand, self-assembles efficiently in solution (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in the mass photometry data in Figure 6B.

claim: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features compared to WT.
source: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features, while G4W does not form polymers; scale bar = 100 nm.
evidence: This is shown in AFM images in Figure 6C.

claim: G4W does not form polymers.
source: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features, while G4W does not form polymers; scale bar = 100 nm.
evidence: This is shown in AFM images in Figure 6C.

claim: I9A forms membrane pores.
source: I9A CL forms membrane pores, while pores were not observed for G4W; scale bars = 100 nm for full images, 10 nm for inset.
evidence: This is shown in AFM images of membranes in Figure 6F.

claim: Pores were not observed for G4W.
source: I9A CL forms membrane pores, while pores were not observed for G4W; scale bars = 100 nm for full images, 10 nm for inset.
evidence: This is shown in AFM images of membranes in Figure 6F.

claim: G4W did not induce membrane disruption in the liposome dye release assay.
source: Figure 6G shows the kinetics of membrane disruption caused by the addition of WT and the two CL variants. We observed that G4W did not induce membrane disruption, in agreement with the lack of membrane pores observed by AFM.
evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claim: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes in the liposome dye release assay.
source: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes, but I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity, as expected from the high loop formation probability (Figure 6E) and the presence of larger membrane pores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claim: I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity.
source: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes, but I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity, as expected from the high loop formation probability (Figure 6E) and the presence of larger membrane pores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claim: G4W showed reduced helical structure in solution and in the presence of POPC liposomes.
source: CD revealed that G4W showed reduced helical structure in solution and in the presence of POPC liposomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in CD data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: I9A displayed higher levels of oligomeric intermediates on SDS-PAGE.
source: When we performed SDS-PAGE of the variants, we observed that I9A displayed higher levels of oligomeric intermediates (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is shown in the SDS-PAGE gel in Figure 6H.

claim: The higher tendency of I9A to polymerize is due to its enhanced oligomerization ability.
source: This result suggests that the higher tendency of I9A to polymerize is due to its enhanced oligomerization ability.
evidence: This is inferred from the SDS-PAGE data showing higher oligomer levels for I9A.

claim: G4W displayed similar levels of oligomers as WT on SDS-PAGE.
source: G4W, on the other hand, displayed similar levels of oligomers as WT.
evidence: This is shown in the SDS-PAGE gel in Figure 6H.

claim: A tryptophan at the N-terminus might impair the ability of two oligomers to bind.
source: We therefore speculate that a W present at the Nt might impair the ability of two oligomers to bind.
evidence: This is speculation based on the G4W mutation data.

claim: Formation of polymers in solution is a necessary step for the formation of membrane pores.
source: The results of the loss-of-function G4W variant revealed that formation of polymers in solution is a necessary step for the formation of membrane pores.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the G4W data showing no polymerization and no pore formation.

claim: CL pores damage the plasma membrane of epithelial cells.
source: CL pores damage the plasma membrane of epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the cellular assay data.

claim: CL attack triggers the activation of danger response signaling, which induces phosphorylation of MAPK phosphatase 1 (MKP1) and subsequent overexpression of the transcription factor c-Fos.
source: This attack triggers the activation of danger response signaling, which induces phosphorylation of MAPK phosphatase 1 (MKP1) and subsequent overexpression of the transcription factor c-Fos (Richardson et al., 2018b; Richardson et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Richardson et al., 2018a and 2018b.

claim: WT CL induced robust increases in c-Fos (threefold) levels and phosphorylation of MKP1 (5-fold) in TR146 cells.
source: When we treated the oral epithelial cell line TR146 with WT CL, we observed robust increases in c-Fos (threefold) levels and phosphorylation of MKP1 (5-fold) (Figure 7), as expected (Moyes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 7.

claim: The I9A variant induced strong MKP1 phosphorylation and significantly higher c-Fos expression than WT.
source: The I9A variant also induced strong MKP1 phosphorylation, but significantly higher c-Fos expression.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 7.

claim: Mutations that alter polymerization impact epithelial cell damage response signaling.
source: Our data therefore indicate that mutations that alter polymerization impact epithelial cell damage response signaling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the cellular assay data for the variants.

claim: Polymerization of CL in solution is a major factor defining C. albicans infection.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that polymerization of CL in solution is a major factor defining C. albicans infection.
evidence: This conclusion integrates biophysical and cellular data.

claim: Pore-forming toxins (PFTs) are typically released as soluble monomers that later bind to the target lipid bilayer.
source: PFTs are typically released as soluble monomers that later bind to the target lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PFT mechanisms.

claim: After membrane binding, PFT monomers find each other and oligomerize.
source: After membrane binding, PFT monomers find each other and oligomerize (Leung et al., 2014; Verma et al., 2021), often forming membrane-anchored pre-pores that later transition into the mature pores that permeabilize membranes (Mondal and Chattopadhyay, 2020; De Schutter et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies on PFT mechanisms.

claim: CL follows a different molecular mechanism for pore formation than typical PFTs.
source: Here, we show that CL follows a different molecular mechanism for pore formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: CL forms both linear and closed loop polymers before binding to the membrane.
source: Multiple lines of evidence indicate that CL forms both linear and closed loop polymers before binding to the membrane (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by TEM, AFM, and other biophysical data.

claim: Closed loop CL polymers insert into lipid bilayers to cause membrane damage without any observable conformational change.
source: Further, acting as soluble pre-pores, closed loop CL polymers insert into lipid bilayers to cause membrane damage without any observable conformational change.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM data showing similar structures for loops in solution and unrimmed pores in membranes.

claim: CL assembles into intermediate size membrane pores, of diameter ≤80 Å.
source: AFM imaging revealed that CL (3.3 kDa) assembles into intermediate size membrane pores, of diameter ≤80 Å, deduced from area distribution peaks <50 nm2 (Figures 5A and 3C) and assuming circularity, which matched many of the pores observed.
evidence: This is calculated from AFM area measurements.

claim: The CL pore diameter is smaller than pores formed by gasdermin-D, suilysin and perfringolysin O.
source: This diameter is smaller than the well-studied aqueous pores formed by the proteins gasdermin-D (Mulvihill et al., 2018), suilysin (Leung et al., 2014) and perfringolysin O (Ramachandran et al., 2002; Czajkowsky et al., 2004), of molecular weights in the 50–60 kDa range, but is probably larger than pores formed by α-hemolysin (diameter: 14–46 Å, 33 kDa) (Song et al., 1996).
evidence: This comparison is made with cited literature on other pore-forming proteins.

claim: CL unrimmed pores present no features above the upper leaflet of the bilayer.
source: In contrast, CL unrimmed pores present no features above the upper leaflet of the bilayer.
evidence: This is observed in AFM images of unrimmed pores.

claim: Unrimmed pores are topographically similar to structures induced by the antimicrobial peptide melittin and its derivatives.
source: Instead, these dynamic structures appear topographically similar to those induced by the antimicrobial peptide melittin and its derivatives (Pittman et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison is made with cited literature on melittin.

claim: Rimmed CL pores are more stable on the timescale of AFM imaging (>0.1 s) than unrimmed pores.
source: Not only are they more stable on the timescale of AFM imaging (>0.1 s), but rimmed pores have a punctate pattern about their periphery.
evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging.

claim: The pore rims arise when the ends of the TM helices of the 8-mer stick out of the bilayer surface upon 90 degree rotation of the 8-mer.
source: This height corresponds to the difference between the 8-mer (4.6 nm) and the DOPC bilayer thickness (4.0 nm, as measured by AFM, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This observation suggests that the pore rims arise when the ends of the TM helices of the 8-mer stick out of the bilayer surface upon 90 degree rotation of the 8-mer in the unrimmed pore, which transitions from the head-to-toe into the side-to-side arrangement (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from AFM measurements and modeling.

claim: Maturation into rimmed pores occurs progressively and is not an all-or-none process.
source: This observation suggests that maturation into rimmed pores occurs progressively and is not an all-or-none process.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations of partially rimmed pores.

claim: The rearrangement of the 8-mer orientation that leads to rim formation causes CL to protrude from the bilayer.
source: In contrast, the rearrangement of the 8-mer orientation that leads to rim formation causes CL to protrude from the bilayer and could be defined as a vertical swell between the two types of pores.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and AFM observations.

claim: In the unrimmed pores, the head-to-toe orientation of the 8-mers would likely place the positive charges of the K side chain in contact with lipid molecules, resulting in a meta-stable configuration.
source: In the unrimmed pores, the head-to-toe orientation of the 8-mers would likely place the positive charges of the K side chain in contact with lipid molecules, resulting in a meta-stable configuration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model and the position of lysine residues.

claim: In the vertical 8-mer orientation found in the rimmed pore, the K residues are expected to be solvent-exposed, resulting in a more stable conformation.
source: However, in the vertical 8-mer orientation found in the rimmed pore, the K residues are expected to be solvent-exposed, resulting in a more stable conformation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model.

claim: Linear CL polymers insert into the membranes but cannot be readily observed as they do not disturb the bilayer surface or protrude significantly from it.
source: However, bilayer removal revealed that linear CL polymers insert into the membranes, but they cannot be readily observed as they do not disturb the bilayer surface or protrude significantly from it.
evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations after detergent treatment.

claim: The assembly of CL into an insertion-competent state in solution might provide an infectivity advantage for C. albicans.
source: The assembly of CL into an insertion-competent state in solution might provide an infectivity advantage for C. albicans, as it could facilitate faster membrane damage.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of the mechanism.

claim: Drug molecules that prevent CL polymerization in solution could be used as therapeutics to fight C. albicans infection.
source: However, drug molecules that prevent CL polymerization in solution could be used as therapeutics to fight C. albicans infection.
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic strategy based on the mechanism.

claim: A molecule that inhibits the formation of CL loops would be expected to prevent the assembly of the membrane pores that damage human epithelial cells.
source: Specifically, a molecule that inhibits the formation of CL loops would be expected to prevent the assembly of the membrane pores that damage human epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism showing that loops become pores.

claim: The basic structural unit in CL polymer formation is likely a CL 8-mer.
source: Our data suggest that the oligomeric state of the basic assembly unit is a CL 8-mer, as indicated by the native mass spectrometry data and this assignment is consistent with AFM volume analysis.
evidence: This is supported by IM-MS data and AFM volume analysis, but acknowledged as challenging to determine precisely.

claim: It cannot be ruled out that CL assembles through an intermediate of different stoichiometry (e.g., a 7-mer or a 9-mer).
source: However, it is intrinsically challenging to precisely determine the stoichiometry of large oligomeric assemblies. We therefore cannot rule out that CL assembles instead through an intermediate of different stoichiometry (e.g., a 7-mer or a 9-mer).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the stoichiometry determination.

claim: CL polymerization represents a novel therapeutic target to treat candidiasis.
source: Our investigation not only unravels a new paradigm for the formation of membrane pores, but additionally identifies CL polymerization as a novel therapeutic target to treat candidiasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the therapeutic implications of the findings.

claim: I9A forms larger membrane pores than WT CL.
source: Consistent with the model that loops in solution become pores, we observed that I9A formed larger membrane pores than WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), while we did not observe membrane pores formed by G4W (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in AFM data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The higher I9A pore area has a corresponding increase in the inner area of the loops compared to WT CL.
source: Additionally, the higher I9A pore area has a corresponding increase in the inner area of the loops compared to WT CL (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the hypothesis that the pore architecture is defined by the loops.
evidence: This is shown in AFM data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unrimmed pores contain six to eight head-to-toe 8-mers.
source: Specifically, the modeled areas predict that unrimmed pores contain six to eight head-to-toe 8-mers, while rimmed pores are formed by six to twelve side-to-side 8-mers.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison between modeling and experimental AFM data.

claim: Rimmed pores are formed by six to twelve side-to-side 8-mers.
source: Specifically, the modeled areas predict that unrimmed pores contain six to eight head-to-toe 8-mers, while rimmed pores are formed by six to twelve side-to-side 8-mers.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison between modeling and experimental AFM data.

claim: In rimmed pores, the 8-mer subunits rotate 90 degrees, switching from the head-to-toe to the side-by-side arrangement.
source: Therefore, we propose that a rimmed pore (Figure 3B) appears when the 8-mer subunits in an unrimmed pore rotate 90 degrees, switching from the head-to-toe to the side-by-side arrangement (compare insets in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on AFM data and modeling.
